passages.title: Mangroves: forests of the tide
paras: Along tropical and subtropical coastlines, where rivers meet the sea, grow some of the most remarkable forests on Earth. Mangroves are trees and shrubs that can survive in salt water, a feat that would kill almost any other woody plant. They are found in more than 120 countries, but they cover only a tiny fraction of the planet’s surface. Despite this, scientists now regard them as one of the most valuable ecosystems on the coast, both for wildlife and for people.

The word ‘mangrove’ does not refer to a single family of plants. Around seventy species are recognised, belonging to several unrelated groups that have each adapted to life between the tides. What they share is not a common ancestor but a common way of life. The richest variety is found in South-East Asia, where a single estuary may contain more than thirty species, each occupying a slightly different zone depending on how often it is flooded and how salty the water is. Species that tolerate the most salt tend to grow nearest the sea, while others are found further up the river, where the water is more diluted.

The first challenge for any plant growing in the sea is salt. Mangroves deal with it in several ways. Some species block most of the salt at their roots, using a filtering system so efficient that the water reaching their leaves is almost fresh. Others allow salt to enter but then get rid of it through special glands on the surface of their leaves; on a dry day, crystals of salt can be seen shining on the leaves of these species. A third group stores the salt in older leaves, which then turn yellow and fall off, taking the salt with them.

The second challenge is oxygen. Mangroves grow in thick mud that is flooded twice a day by the tide, and this mud contains almost no oxygen. To solve this problem, many mangroves have developed roots that grow upwards out of the mud, like pencils pointing at the sky. These roots, known as pneumatophores, are covered in tiny openings that take in air when the tide is low. Other species have arching roots that support the tree like the legs of a table and also absorb oxygen.

Mangroves also have an unusual way of reproducing. In many species, the seed begins to grow while it is still attached to the parent tree, producing a long, pointed seedling. When it finally drops, it may stick straight into the mud below and begin growing immediately. If it lands in the water instead, it can float for months, travelling long distances on ocean currents until it reaches a suitable shore.

For coastal communities, mangroves provide a natural defence. Their dense roots slow down waves and hold sediment in place, reducing erosion. Studies carried out after the Indian Ocean tsunami of 2004 suggested that villages behind healthy mangrove forests suffered less damage than those where the forests had been cleared, although researchers warn that mangroves cannot provide complete protection against very large waves.

Mangroves are also nurseries for the sea. The calm, shallow water among their roots offers shelter to young fish, crabs and shrimps, protecting them from larger predators. Many of the fish later caught in the open ocean spent the first part of their lives in mangroves, so the health of these forests has a direct effect on local fishing industries.

Perhaps their most important role, however, is in the fight against climate change. Mangroves absorb carbon dioxide from the air and store it in their roots and in the waterlogged soil beneath them, where it can remain for thousands of years. Hectare for hectare, mangrove forests can store up to four times as much carbon as tropical rainforests.

Unfortunately, mangroves have been disappearing at an alarming rate. Over the last half century, around a third of the world’s mangroves have been lost, cleared mainly to make space for shrimp farms, rice fields and tourist developments. When the trees are removed, the carbon stored in the soil is released, adding to the problem of global warming. In recent years, however, many countries have begun replanting programmes. Early projects often failed because the wrong species were planted in the wrong places, but scientists have learned from these mistakes, and the rate of loss has now slowed considerably.

passages.title: The hidden cost of city noise
paras: Noise is so much a part of city life that most people hardly notice it. Traffic, construction work, aircraft and loud music combine to create a constant background of sound. Yet according to the World Health Organization, noise is the second most harmful environmental factor to health in Europe, after air pollution. In recent decades, researchers have begun to measure exactly how this invisible pollutant affects our bodies and minds.

The most obvious effect of noise is on sleep. Even when we do not wake up, sudden noises during the night cause our heart rate to rise and our bodies to release stress hormones. Professor Anna Lindgren, who has studied people living near airports, found that many residents claimed to have become used to the sound of night flights. However, measurements of their blood pressure told a different story: their bodies were still reacting to every plane, even though they were not aware of it.

Over many years, these repeated stress responses can have serious consequences. Long-term exposure to traffic noise has been linked to high blood pressure, heart disease and strokes. One large study estimated that, in western Europe alone, more than a million healthy years of life are lost every year as a result of traffic noise. The risks are greatest for people whose bedrooms face a busy road.

Noise also affects learning. In a well-known study, Dr Michael Haines compared children attending schools near a major airport with children at quieter schools. He found that the children exposed to aircraft noise had poorer reading skills and long-term memory. Importantly, when one airport closed and another opened, the reading skills of children near the old airport improved, while those of children near the new one declined. Haines argued that this showed that noise was the cause of the difference, rather than other factors such as family income.

Not all sound is harmful, however. Researchers have found that natural sounds, such as birdsong, running water and the wind in the trees, can actually reduce stress. Dr Laura Okafor asked volunteers to complete a stressful task and then listen to either traffic noise or recordings of nature. Those who heard natural sounds recovered more quickly, and their heart rates returned to normal sooner. Okafor believes that the human brain is designed to find such sounds reassuring, because they signalled a safe environment to our ancestors.

So what can cities do? Some solutions are technical: quieter road surfaces, which can reduce traffic noise by up to ten decibels, and barriers along motorways. Electric vehicles are also quieter at low speeds, although at higher speeds most of the noise comes from tyres rather than engines. Other approaches focus on planning. Professor Daniel Reyes, an urban designer, argues that cities should protect ‘quiet areas’ such as parks and courtyards, where residents can escape the noise. In his view, it is not necessary to make the whole city silent; what matters is that everyone has access to a quiet place within a short walk of their home.

Some cities have begun to take noise more seriously. Paris has installed ‘noise radars’ that identify vehicles that are too loud, and the owners can be fined. Other cities have created noise maps, showing which streets are the loudest, so that new housing can be planned in quieter areas. Although such measures remain unusual, many experts believe that, within a generation, people will regard noise in the same way they now regard smoking in public places: as an unnecessary harm that should not be tolerated.

passages.title: Can we trust our memories?
paras: Most of us believe that our memories, at least of important events, are a fairly accurate record of what happened. We may forget details, we admit, but the main facts remain. Research carried out over the past fifty years suggests that this confidence is misplaced. Memory, it turns out, is not like a video recording that can be played back. Each time we recall an event, we rebuild it, and in doing so we may change it.

Some of the clearest evidence comes from studies of so-called ‘flashbulb memories’, the vivid recollections people have of where they were when they heard shocking news. The day after a major disaster in the United States, a group of researchers asked students to write down how they had heard the news. Two and a half years later, they asked the same students again. Many of the later accounts were completely different from the originals, yet the students were extremely confident that their memories were correct. Some, when shown their original accounts, insisted that these must be wrong.

Memory researchers often distinguish between the ‘gist’ of an event and its details. We tend to keep the general meaning of an experience, such as the fact that a meeting was tense or a holiday was enjoyable, while the specific details fade quickly. When we try to recall those details later, the brain fills the gaps with what seems likely, drawing on our knowledge of similar situations. Usually this works well enough. The difficulty is that the invented details feel exactly the same as the genuine ones, so we have no way of telling them apart from the inside.

In the 1970s, the psychologist Elizabeth Loftus showed how easily memories can be influenced by the way questions are asked. Volunteers watched a film of a car accident and were then asked how fast the cars were going when they ‘hit’ or ‘smashed into’ each other. Those who heard the word ‘smashed’ gave higher estimates of speed. A week later, they were also more likely to report seeing broken glass, although there had been none in the film. Later studies went further, showing that it is possible to make people remember entire events that never happened, such as being lost in a shopping centre as a child.

These findings have serious implications for the legal system, where the evidence of eyewitnesses has traditionally been given great weight. In the United States, studies of cases in which people were later proved innocent by DNA evidence have found that mistaken eyewitness identification played a part in around seventy per cent of them. In my view, this is not because witnesses are dishonest; they genuinely believe what they say. The problem is that a confident witness is very persuasive, and juries tend to assume that confidence is a sign of accuracy, which, as we have seen, it is not.

Some changes have been made as a result. Police in many countries now follow procedures designed to avoid influencing witnesses, for example by having identity parades conducted by an officer who does not know which person is the suspect. Witnesses are asked to state how confident they are immediately, before their memory can be affected by later information. These are sensible reforms, but they are not yet used everywhere, and I believe they should be required by law.

It would be easy to conclude from all this that memory is simply unreliable, but that would be a mistake. Our memories are generally good enough for everyday purposes, and the flexibility that makes them vulnerable to error may also be useful. Some researchers argue that the ability to recombine pieces of past experience is exactly what allows us to imagine the future and plan for situations we have never faced. If memory were a perfect recording, we might be less able to adapt.

What, then, should we do with our own memories? Not, I think, abandon them, but hold them a little more loosely. When two people remember the same event differently, it is tempting to assume that one of them is lying. The research suggests that both may be sincere, and both may be partly wrong. Recognising this might make us not only better witnesses, but also more patient with each other.
